name: Fatima Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don’t sell anything or campaign. Your answers are confidential. Could you describe an ordinary workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Fatima Okafor, 27, and I lead a line crew for an electricity company. At the east depot I check the outage board, mark the access road in orange on our printed map, and then we head out to inspect or repair overhead lines.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about that work, and what is hardest?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like solving a problem with the crew and knowing that people have power again before they get home. Night call-outs are tiring, but I earn higher pay than the job average and have more than six months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a report assistant can clean up the outage log, but the crew still checks the pole before closing a job. I use AI to find a manual quickly, though the safety call stays with the qualified worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my line work and pay remain steady in this version. My reserve covers a slow month, so I’m not worrying about a small change to paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d compare the report assistant’s notes with the crew’s marked map for several weeks and tell the supervisor where it misses an access hazard. I’d keep my shifts and savings transfer as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm because the tool saves a little office time, not the climb. I still want every hazard checked before anyone signs a permit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the report marked a road as open when it was blocked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d stop the dispatch and correct the route with the control desk before the crew drove out. Then I’d add the closure to our printed map so the next shift sees it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a better version yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the employer should buy work tools and make sure they are safe. I’d keep my savings for my own plans and leave purchasing decisions to the people who run the budget.

say: I’d say an assistant can clean **outage logs**, but the crew still checks each pole.
I use AI to find manuals, while **safety calls** stay with workers.
think: I think my **line work** and pay remain steady in this small-change picture.
My reserve covers a slow month, so **paperwork changes** do not worry me.
do: Compare assistant notes with the **marked crew map** for several weeks.
Keep my current **line shifts** and savings transfer.
Correct **blocked-road information** before dispatching the crew.
feel: I feel **calm**, because this tool does not change the climb.
S0.quote: I still want every hazard checked before anyone signs a permit.
fieldNote: Fatima uses AI as a **reference aid**, while keeping access and safety decisions with the crew.
Higher pay and **strong savings** make this small change financially secure.

steps.text: Compare assistant notes with the marked crew map for several weeks
Keep the usual line shifts and check access details before dispatch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the system can sort routes and stock orders, but it has to show crews what changed and why. I’d ask the union to include lineworkers in the trial before a new schedule becomes the rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I handle planning and reports when I lead, so some of those duties could be reduced. There are plenty of utilities nearby and my savings are solid, but I still need to know whether my paid lead hours stay the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d learn the new dispatch system and compare its route suggestions with what the crew finds on site. I’d join the union trial group and ask management to publish the effect on paid lead hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy because part of my lead role is thinking work, but I have time and options. I want the people who carry the risk to help set the process, not just receive it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a useful trial result?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d count wrong routes, missed access notes and repeated safety corrections, not just time saved. I’d also compare how many lead hours and field inspections remain after the trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start applying to other utilities now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d wait for the trial report and staffing plan, since I have choices nearby and a financial cushion. If a real vacancy appeared, I’d compare its duties and hours with what I have now.

say: I’d say the system must explain **route changes** to the crews.
I’d ask the union to include lineworkers in the **dispatch trial**.
think: I think some **planning and reporting** in my lead role could shrink.
I need to know whether my **paid hours** stay the same, despite local options.
do: Learn the **dispatch system** and compare its routes with site results.
Join the union trial group and request **published lead-hour data**.
Wait for a **staffing plan** before applying elsewhere.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, because some duties may shrink but I have time and options.
S1.quote: I want the people who carry the risk to help set the process, not just receive it.
fieldNote: She sees **planning exposure** but expects local employers and savings to provide options.
Her response combines **early tool learning** with worker involvement in trial rules.

steps.text: Learn the dispatch system and compare route suggestions with sites

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI can take planning, records and diagnosis by 2028, and robots reach hands-on work around 2031. I’d want clear staffing terms and paid training before an employer says workers should simply adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my planning duties to disappear and my lead hours to shrink first. I have enough savings and nearby employers to look around, but I don’t know whether another job will pay what I earn now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d use the two years to complete a recognized electrical safety instructor course while keeping my current pay. In 2029 I’d apply to actual field or training openings, checking the duties because AGI can also plan, teach and diagnose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious because I expect my lead duties to change, although I have a cushion and time to look. I would not assume that a higher-paying post is waiting at another company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want a transition agreement to include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want paid course time, advance notice of crew reductions and a list of real vacancies. I’d also want a worker to sign off on safety instructions that an automated system produces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could training or inspection become a safe career after full AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I can’t call those jobs safe because they use planning, lesson writing and diagnosis. I’d consider a real opening as a possible next step, not a guarantee that income is protected.

say: I’d say AGI can take **planning and diagnosis** by 2028.
I’d ask for staffing terms and **paid training** before cuts begin.
think: I expect my **planning duties to disappear** and lead hours to shrink.
I can search, but I don’t know if another job matches my **current pay**.
do: Complete a recognized **electrical safety instructor course** before 2028.
Apply to real field or training openings in **2029** and check duties.
Request **paid course time** and written transition terms.
feel: I feel **anxious about lead hours**, though my savings and local options help.
S2.quote: I would not assume that a higher-paying post is waiting at another company.
fieldNote: Fatima expects **lead-hour reductions**, while strong reserves and nearby firms give her room to search.
She refuses to label **training or inspection protected** after the AGI date.

steps.text: Complete a recognized electrical safety instructor course
Apply for actual field or training openings in 2029
Ask the union to negotiate paid training and transition notice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years is enough to train and negotiate, but not enough to treat the current lead role as permanent. Thinking tasks change in 2031, and the robot date reaches line work in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build a better plan and compare employers without racing to leave my current job. I still expect planning and records to be taken over, and a trainer position could be changed by AGI as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the union for a written directory of local utilities with practical training roles. In 2032 I’d apply where duties and wages are posted, and I’d set aside money for a move only after I had an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about losing lead work, but I have time to check the market and a strong reserve. I would rather negotiate a fair transition than let each worker handle a cut on their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What local rule would you ask policymakers to consider?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for a rule that requires a qualified worker’s sign-off on safety-critical automated instructions. I’d write the local representative and ask them to support that standard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you organize around that with your union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I’d take the proposal to the union meeting and ask for it to be part of negotiations. Workers should see the safety record and staffing plan before the system becomes standard.

say: I’d say five years allows **training and negotiation**, not permanent protection.
I expect thinking tasks to change in 2031 and line work in **2034**.
think: I can compare employers without **rushing to leave** my current job.
I expect records to be automated, and **trainer work** may change too.
do: Ask the union for a **directory of training roles**.
Apply to posted openings in **2032** and compare duties and wages.
Write the local representative about **worker sign-off rules**.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but have time to compare courses and vacancies.
S3.quote: I would rather negotiate a fair transition than let each worker handle a cut on their own.
fieldNote: She uses financial room to **compare employers**, while expecting lead work to be automated.
She connects safety concerns to **union rules** and public standards that clarify employer responsibility.

steps.text: Apply to posted openings in 2032 after comparing duties and wages
Ask the local representative to support worker sign-off rules
Bring safety concerns to union negotiations

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years gives crews time to train and negotiate a responsible change, but the employer should start sharing plans now. AGI reaches planning in 2036, then robots reach physical work around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can keep my income and savings while taking training in stages and checking what jobs are real. I still expect my line work to change eventually, and I won’t count on a desk role surviving full AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d complete the practical instructor course in sections and add a fixed amount to savings each month, keeping the reserve above six months of expenses. In 2037 I’d compare actual openings at nearby utilities and apply when the duties and wages are clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because I can prepare, but I still expect the robot date to reach my physical work. My higher pay and savings let me make choices without pretending that the job stays unchanged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the union to do over that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want it to negotiate paid learning time, worker sign-off and clear notice of staffing changes. I’d support a public rule for safety-critical instructions so every employer has to show who is accountable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could instructor or inspection work remain safe forever?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, both roles use planning and diagnosis, so I wouldn’t call them safe after AGI. I’d compare them with actual openings and keep preparing for robots to affect field work in 2039.

say: I’d say ten years gives us time to **train and negotiate responsibly**.
I expect AGI to reach planning in 2036 and robots in **2039**.
think: I can keep my income while **training in stages**.
I expect line work to change and won’t rely on a **desk role**.
do: Complete the practical **instructor course** in sections.
Add a fixed monthly amount to keep savings above **six months** of expenses.
Compare nearby openings in **2037** and apply when wages are clear.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, because I can prepare but still expect change.
S4.quote: My higher pay and savings let me make choices without pretending that the job stays unchanged.
fieldNote: The long horizon lets her **prepare while earning**, but she expects a later robot impact.
She prioritizes **worker sign-off** and shared accountability for safety instructions.

steps.text: Complete the practical electrical instructor course in sections

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because there is little time before planning changes and robots arrive in 2031. Paid learning time, written staffing plans and a worker sign-off rule would help crews prepare and share responsibility.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is accountable when a system changes the safety instructions. I want lineworkers and their union included before a new rule reaches the job site.

headlineQuote: I want lineworkers and their union included before a new rule reaches the job site.
portrait: Fatima is a **crew lead** who uses AI for reference but keeps safety calls with workers.
She earns **higher pay** and has more than six months of expenses saved.
She favors **union oversight** and public safety rules for new systems.
Strong local options and savings let her plan carefully, though she expects **robots** to reach physical work.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** leaves little time before planning changes and robots arrive in 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid learning time**, written staffing plans and worker sign-off rules would help crews prepare.
